hub.description: Decks and fences for Mount Juliet, TN homes, from bare new build yards in HOA subdivisions to sloped lots along Old Hickory Lake.
hub.intro: Many Mount Juliet homes are fairly new, and the back yard often shows it. You might have open lawn with no fence, a small concrete patio at the back door, or a builder grade deck that feels cramped once a table is on it. Homes closer to Old Hickory Lake bring other questions, like how steep the yard is and where the lot actually ends. This page is a short overview of what shapes deck and fence work in Mount Juliet, with links to the full page for each.

sections.heading: New subdivisions and the yards that come with them
paragraphs: Mount Juliet has grown fast, and much of that growth has come as new subdivisions, many of them with an HOA. When a builder finishes a house, the yard usually gets sod plus a small patio or a basic deck. A fence is rarely included. That means a lot of Mount Juliet homeowners start with open grass and not much else.

New Mount Juliet yards come with a few quirks worth knowing. Soil near the foundation was dug out and pushed back during construction, so it can be softer than the ground farther out. Lots are usually graded to move water toward a swale on the back or side line, which is often right where a fence would go. Young trees mean little shade, so a new deck in Mount Juliet may sit in direct sun most of the afternoon.

sections.heading: Homes on the slope down to Old Hickory Lake
paragraphs: Old Hickory Lake runs along the north side of Mount Juliet, and homes near it often sit on ground that falls toward the water. On those lots a deck off the main floor can stand well above the yard, with long posts and a tall run of stairs. A fence on the same slope has to step down the hill or follow it, and either way the bottom edge needs attention so pets cannot slip under.

The shoreline raises its own question. Around much of Old Hickory Lake, the land right along the water is federal property that the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers manages, and it is not part of the private lot beside it. Fences and decks generally are not allowed on that land without Corps permission. If your Mount Juliet yard runs toward the lake, find your boundary on the survey before you plan anything near the water.

sections.heading: Decks for Mount Juliet homes
paragraphs: Deck work in Mount Juliet tends to fall into two groups. One is replacing or enlarging the small deck a builder added to a newer house. The other is building a deck where there is only a patio or a door with a short set of steps. Both start below the boards, with footings dug into firm soil and a solid connection to the house. Our [deck builder page for Mount Juliet](/deck-builder-mount-juliet-tn/) goes deeper on footings in new build dirt and on decks for lake lots.

sections.heading: Fences for Mount Juliet yards
paragraphs: Fence projects in Mount Juliet usually start with privacy or a dog. Houses in newer Mount Juliet subdivisions sit fairly close together, so a privacy fence along the back and sides makes a real difference in how the yard feels. The planning starts with your plat, which shows the lot lines and any easements along them. Neighbors also fence at different times, so it helps to decide early how your fence will meet theirs. The [Mount Juliet fence company page](/fence-company-mount-juliet-tn/) goes through setting posts in local clay and rock, along with HOA rules.

sections.heading: Approval and permits before anyone digs
paragraphs: Many Mount Juliet subdivisions have an HOA, and most HOAs want to review a deck or fence before it goes up. Whether you live in Providence or on a street closer to the lake, check whether covenants apply to your lot before you plan. Expect to send a drawing that shows placement on the lot along with the material and color. Some review committees meet only on a set schedule, so approval can take a while. Our guide to [getting HOA approval for a fence or deck](/guides/hoa-approval-deck-fence/) shows how to put together a clean submission.

Permits are a separate step. A Mount Juliet mailing address does not always mean the house is inside city limits, and homes in unincorporated Wilson County go through the county instead of the city. Deck and fence rules can differ between the two, so confirm with the codes office that covers your address. Before any digging, call Tennessee 811 so buried utility lines get marked.

faqs.q: How do I know if my home is inside Mount Juliet city limits?
faqs.a: Your mailing address will not always tell you. Some homes with a Mount Juliet address sit in unincorporated Wilson County. The quickest answer is to call the city or county codes office and give them your address. It matters because the permit office, and sometimes the rules for decks and fences, depend on which side of the line your lot falls.

faqs.q: Can I build a deck or fence all the way to Old Hickory Lake?
faqs.a: Usually not all the way. On many lake lots in the Mount Juliet area, the land nearest the water is federal property managed by the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers. Private decks and fences are generally not allowed there without Corps permission. Your survey or plat shows where your lot stops. Plan the project inside that line, and take any question about the shoreline strip to the Corps directly.

faqs.q: What should I have ready before asking for an estimate?
faqs.a: A copy of your plat or survey is the most useful thing, since it shows lot lines and easements. If you have an HOA, keep its deck and fence rules handy. A few photos from the back door and from the far corners of the yard show the slope. With those in hand, it is easier to price your actual yard. When you are ready, [request an estimate](#estimate) below.

deck.description: Deck builder in Mount Juliet, TN for replacing small builder decks, adding a deck beside a bare patio, and building on sloped Old Hickory Lake lots.
deck.intro: Many deck projects in Mount Juliet start with a fairly new house. The builder left a small deck with a narrow set of stairs, or just a concrete pad under the back door, and neither one holds a table and a grill at the same time. Homes near Old Hickory Lake have a different problem, with yards that drop toward the water. Whether you live in Willoughby Station or Nichols Vale, the sections below cover what to sort out before a deck goes up.

sections.heading: Replacing the builder deck on a Mount Juliet home
paragraphs: Builder grade decks tend to look alike. They are small, often with room for two chairs and not much else. The stairs often drop straight down wherever they were easiest to frame. Boards and railings are usually basic pressure treated lumber, and after a few Tennessee summers they start to gray and check. Nothing about that is wrong, but plenty of Mount Juliet homeowners outgrow it quickly.

The first thing most people ask is whether the old deck can be extended. Sometimes it can. Often, though, the footings and beams were sized for the small deck alone, and adding on means rebuilding most of the frame anyway. A good deck builder will check how the ledger is fastened to the house and how big the footings are before agreeing to add on. When most of the structure has to change, a new deck is usually the cleaner job. If you are unsure whether yours is worth keeping, our guide on [signs a deck is done](/guides/signs-you-need-a-new-deck/) can help.

sections.heading: Footings in new build dirt and Wilson County rock
paragraphs: The ground around a new Mount Juliet house is not uniform. Right next to the foundation, soil was dug out during construction and pushed back in afterward. That backfill can stay looser than the undisturbed ground farther out, and a footing set in it may settle. Footings near the house often need to go deeper to reach firm soil, while the ones out in the yard may not.

Under the topsoil, many Wilson County yards have clay, with limestone close enough to the surface that an auger can hit it. Clay can swell when it is wet and shrink in dry spells, so footings should go deep enough to get below the soil that moves the most. Rock is a different problem. The fix depends on how solid it is and what the inspector will accept. Ask any deck builder how rock is handled and priced before the job starts, not after.

sections.heading: Decks on the lake side of Mount Juliet
paragraphs: Homes near Old Hickory Lake often sit on ground that slopes down toward the water, and some have a walkout lower level. A deck off the main floor on that side can end up high above the yard. Taller decks need heavier posts and proper bracing, and the stairs may need a landing partway down. Railings have to be safe, and on the lake side many owners pick a style that keeps the water in view.

On a Mount Juliet lake lot, know where your property ends before sketching anything toward the water. A lot of the shoreline around Old Hickory Lake is public land under the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers, and building there without their permission can mean being told to remove the work. Stairs or a lower platform that run past your line are an easy mistake to make. Pull out your survey or plat first, and keep the deck plan inside it.

sections.heading: Getting a Mount Juliet deck approved and permitted
paragraphs: If your Mount Juliet subdivision has an HOA, it very likely reviews decks. Expect to send a drawing of the deck on your plat with its size marked, along with the board and railing colors. Some covenants limit how far a deck can reach into the yard or which stain colors are allowed. Wait for approval in writing before any work begins. Building first and asking later can end with changes you pay for twice.

The building permit is a separate step. Attached decks and raised decks usually need one. Which office you apply to depends on whether your home is inside Mount Juliet city limits or out in unincorporated Wilson County, and a Mount Juliet mailing address does not settle that by itself. In many places, inspections include a footing check before concrete and a final look at the finished deck. Rules vary, so confirm with the codes office for your address. Our guide to [deck permits in Tennessee](/guides/deck-permits-tennessee/) explains the general process.

sections.heading: Boards for a yard with no shade
paragraphs: New lots in Mount Juliet often have no mature trees, so a deck can sit in full sun from late morning until evening. Pressure treated pine is the usual starting point. Pine costs the least, and a damaged board is simple to swap. In hard sun, though, pine checks and splits sooner unless you seal it on a steady schedule, and boards can cup if water sits on them.

Composite boards skip the regular staining and do not rot, but each board costs more. Darker composite colors can get uncomfortably hot for bare feet on a deck that faces the afternoon sun. A lighter shade helps. Before deciding, set a few samples in the sun and touch them. There is more on upkeep and surface heat in our [wood and composite decking comparison](/guides/wood-vs-composite-decking/).

sections.heading: Fitting the deck to the yard you have
paragraphs: Start with what actually happens out back. A grill needs space to stand clear of the house and the railing. Chairs around a table for six need room to slide back. If kids go straight for the grass, the stairs should land toward the play area, not the side yard. Many newer Mount Juliet lots are narrow, so a deck that runs wide along the back of the house usually works better than one that pushes deep into the yard.

The small patio the builder poured does not have to go. A deck can step down onto it, giving you a lower spot for chairs or a small table. Think ahead about where a fence gate will go, too, so the stairs and the gate line up for mowing and trash cans. If a fence is also on your list, our [fence page for Mount Juliet](/fence-company-mount-juliet-tn/) covers that side of the yard.

faqs.q: Can my builder grade deck in Mount Juliet be extended instead of replaced?
faqs.a: Sometimes. It depends on whether the existing footings and beams can carry more than the small deck they hold now. On many newer homes they were built for that deck alone. A deck builder can look at the frame and the ledger and tell you whether adding on is sound. If it is, the new section should match the old one in board color and railing style so the deck does not look patched together.

faqs.q: Do I need HOA approval to build a deck in Mount Juliet?
faqs.a: If an HOA covers your lot, very likely yes, even for a deck that sits low to the ground. Send the HOA or its review committee a drawing that shows placement and size, plus the materials and colors, and wait for written approval before work starts. The city or county building permit is a separate step, so you may need both. Your covenants or the management company can tell you what the review requires.

faqs.q: Is a deck on a steep Mount Juliet lot near Old Hickory Lake harder to build?
faqs.a: It takes more planning and usually more labor. Taller posts need bracing, and carrying materials down a slope slows the work. Footings on the low side end up farther below the deck, so the soil and rock there matter even more. It is very doable, but expect the price to reflect the height and the access. Also confirm your boundary first, since the land along the shore is often Corps property.

faqs.q: Can a deck be built over the patio my builder poured?
faqs.a: It can, if there is enough height between the patio and the door for the framing and boards. The posts still need their own footings in the ground, because a thin patio slab is usually not built to carry that kind of load. Often the better plan is to keep the patio as a lower level and step the deck down onto it. You keep the concrete you already paid for and gain a second spot to sit.

faqs.q: What should a deck builder in Mount Juliet include in a bid?
faqs.a: A clear bid spells out the deck size along with the board and railing materials. It should show where the stairs land and how the footings will be dug, including what happens if the auger hits rock. Look for who handles the permit and the HOA paperwork too, and whether tearing out an old deck is included. When two bids are far apart, compare those lines first. The gap is often something one bid left out.

fence.description: Fence installation in Mount Juliet, TN: privacy fences for new build yards, posts set for clay and rock, and lake lots planned around Corps land.
fence.intro: Many new houses in Mount Juliet come without a fence. On moving day the back yard is open to neighbors on three sides, and if you have a dog, every trip outside means a leash. Fence installation here usually starts with HOA review and a close look at your plat for lot lines and easements. This page covers those steps for Mount Juliet yards, along with what changes when your lot is near Old Hickory Lake.

sections.heading: Fencing a new build yard in Mount Juliet
paragraphs: On a new Mount Juliet street, you are often the first house to fence or one of the last. If you go first, you set the line, and neighbors may tie into your fence later. Going last can mean two or three different fences already standing along your sides and back. Some HOAs want a new fence to match or meet the existing ones cleanly, so look at what is already there before you settle on a style.

New yards also come with fresh grading. Builders shape each lot so water runs toward a swale, often along the back or side line, which is exactly where most people want a fence. Sod laid over new fill can hide soft ground. A careful fence company looks at where water collects after a rain before choosing post locations. In Providence, Nichols Vale or anywhere else, start with the plat or survey in your closing papers.

sections.heading: What HOAs in Mount Juliet usually review
paragraphs: Many subdivisions in Mount Juliet have covenants that cover fences in some detail. Common points are which styles and colors are allowed and how tall a fence may be. Many also say how far back from the front corner of the house a side fence has to start. Some require the finished side to face neighbors and the street. The details differ between neighborhoods, so read your own covenants instead of going by what a friend across town was allowed to build.

Mark the fence line on a copy of your plat and note the style and height. Most committees also want a photo or drawing of the design. Wait for written approval before anyone digs. A fence built without approval can draw a letter asking you to change it or take it down, which costs far more than the wait. Plan the approval time into your schedule if you want the yard closed in by a certain date.

sections.heading: Finding your pins and easements before digging
paragraphs: Before any fence installation, you need to know where the lot lines are. In newer Mount Juliet subdivisions, the metal pins at the corners are often still in place, though they may be buried under sod or mulch. A metal detector often finds them. If they cannot be found, a surveyor can locate or reset them. That costs something, but far less than moving a fence after a neighbor disputes the line.

The plat also shows easements. Drainage and utility easements commonly run along back and side lines. A fence can often be built in one, but the utility may have the right to take it down for access, and replacing it may fall to you. Where a fence crosses a swale, leave room at the bottom so water can pass instead of backing up. Call Tennessee 811 before digging so buried lines are marked. Our guide to [fences and property lines in Tennessee](/guides/fence-property-line-tennessee/) goes into more detail.

sections.heading: Fences on lake lots in Mount Juliet
paragraphs: Mount Juliet yards near Old Hickory Lake bring two questions that lots in the middle of town do not. The first is where your property stops. Along much of the lake, the ground nearest the water belongs to the federal government and is overseen by the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers. A private fence generally cannot run across it. Check your survey for the boundary, and treat anything beyond it as a question for the Corps.

The second question is the view. A solid privacy fence on the water side can block the lake view. Some lake homeowners keep solid panels along the sides for privacy from neighbors and use a lower or more open style facing the lake. These yards also tend to slope toward the water. Panels can step down the hill or follow the grade, and each method leaves a different gap at the bottom. Our guide on [how to fence a sloped yard](/guides/fence-on-a-slope/) compares the two.

sections.heading: Setting posts in Mount Juliet clay and rock
paragraphs: A fence stays straight only as long as its posts do. Much of the ground in Wilson County is heavy clay, and limestone often sits close enough to the surface that a post hole hits rock partway down. Clay holds water after a storm and can shrink away from posts in a dry summer. Over time that movement is a common reason fences lean. Posts need enough depth, and the concrete at the top should slope so water runs away from the wood.

When a hole hits rock, the answer depends on the rock. Broken or layered rock can often be dug through. Solid limestone may need a rock bit, which takes longer and adds to the cost. A fence company should tell you up front how it handles rock so it does not show up as a surprise on the final bill. Near the house on a new Mount Juliet build, loose backfill can mean some posts need extra depth to hold.

sections.heading: Privacy fences for close subdivision lots
paragraphs: In many Mount Juliet subdivisions the houses sit close together, and a privacy fence along the back and sides is what most people want first. A solid wood privacy fence blocks the view at ground level, which covers the patio and the lawn. A neighbor at a second story window will still see over it, and a taller fence may not be allowed by your HOA anyway.

Board on board gives full coverage because the boards overlap, so no gaps open as the wood dries and shrinks. Shadowbox looks the same from both sides and lets some air through, with a little less privacy at an angle. If a dog is part of the plan, keep the bottom close to the ground and make sure gates close and latch on their own. Our look at [privacy fence options](/guides/privacy-fence-options/) compares the common styles.

faqs.q: Does a fence in Mount Juliet need a permit or just HOA approval?
faqs.a: Treat them as two separate questions. The HOA reviews style and placement under your covenants. Whether a building permit is needed depends on where you live and what you plan to build, and the answer can differ between the city of Mount Juliet and unincorporated Wilson County. Call the codes office for your address before scheduling the work, and keep the HOA approval letter somewhere you can find it.

faqs.q: Can my new fence tie into my neighbor's fence?
faqs.a: Often, yes, with your neighbor's agreement. Tying in means your end post sits against theirs or connects to it, so there is no gap for a dog to squeeze through. Ask before the work starts, since the fence you are connecting to belongs to them. Some Mount Juliet HOAs want the two fences to match where they meet. If the existing fence sits off the property line, sort that out before you connect to it.

faqs.q: What happens if my fence goes in a utility easement?
faqs.a: Many Mount Juliet subdivision plats show utility or drainage easements along the back and sides of each lot. A fence can often be built there, but the utility may be able to remove sections if it needs access, and putting them back may be your cost. Some plats and HOAs restrict fences in drainage easements altogether. Read the notes on your plat and ask the HOA before you settle on a line, and put a gate where a crew would need to get in.

faqs.q: How soon after closing on a new Mount Juliet house can I get a fence?
faqs.a: There is usually no need to wait for the yard to settle before fencing. The real wait is paperwork. HOA review can take a while, and a permit may be needed depending on your address. Tennessee 811 also has to mark buried lines before anyone digs. Send your HOA submission soon after closing if you want the yard closed in quickly. Finding your lot corners early helps too.

faqs.q: How should I compare bids from fence companies in Mount Juliet?
faqs.a: Put them side by side, line by line. Look at the post material, how deep the posts go, and how they are set. Then compare the board style and gate hardware, and check whether hauling off an old fence is included. Ask each fence company how it handles rock, since Wilson County ground can surprise you. A bid that is much lower usually leaves something out, often the HOA paperwork or the rock.
